name: Luna
subtitle: every Luna's planet
cover: Luna has no moon. It’s named after one.
beats:
It takes this personally.
Every spring there is a fund-raiser.

The moon fund has raised enough for one lamp.
They point it at the sky on birthdays.
odd_line: The lamp has a waiting list. Birthdays get priority.
story: Luna is named after a moon it has never had, and it takes this very personally. Every spring there is a fund-raiser. So far they have raised enough for one large lamp on a tall pole, which is switched on and pointed at the sky for birthdays, anniversaries and anyone having a bad week.
rule: Do not mention other planets' moons in front of Luna.
question: Know a Luna? This one's theirs.
extra: The lamp has a waiting list. Birthdays get priority.
opener: Named after a moon it doesn't have.

episode.opener:
Luna has no moon.
It’s named after one.

beats.text: It takes this personally.

In 1987, a moon came very close.
It didn’t stop.

Every spring since, a fund-raiser.
They’re getting there.

Meanwhile,
they’ve bought a lamp.

It’s lit for birthdays, anniversaries
and anyone having a bad week.

Mr Okafor keeps the waiting list.
‘Birthdays first. No exceptions.’
Once a year, he makes one.

episode.caption:
Watch the sign by the lamp.

Luna is named after a moon it has never had. In the autumn of 1987 one came very close, slowed down, and kept going. Nobody says its name. It knows what it did.

The Moon Fund has met every spring since: bake sales, a sponsored silence, one raffle that got out of hand. It stands at 3%. Meanwhile there's the lamp, on a forty-metre pole on the hill above town. When it comes on, the whole town goes 'ooh'. Every time. Mr Okafor keeps the waiting list in a ring binder at the post office. Bad weeks are on the honour system. The night it's booked for Luna is the anniversary. Nobody mentions that either.

Local rule: do not mention other planets' moons in front of Luna. Especially Luma's.

Every Luna is on the list. For life.

first_comment: Moon Fund update: 3% is now 3.1%. Mrs Okafor's sponsored silence went very well. Nobody could tell.

name: Max
subtitle: every Max's planet
beats: Everything on Max is set to maximum. The rivers, the sun, the birds.
The quiet setting was removed by public vote. The vote was very loud.
odd_line: The library is the loudest building on the planet. It had to compete.
story: Everything on Max is set to maximum. The rivers run at full volume, the sun is on its brightest setting, and the birds know one song, which is loud. There used to be a quiet setting. It was removed by public vote, and the vote was also very loud. The library is now the noisiest building on the planet, because it had to compete.
question: Know a Max? Is this accurate?
extra: Bedtime is set to maximum too. It hasn't been reached yet.

episode.opener:
Nothing here has
a quiet setting.

beats.text:
There used to be one.
It was removed by public vote.
The vote was very loud.

Even the library is loud.
It had to compete.

Whispering requires a licence.
You apply by shouting.

Only one was ever issued,
to Nell, aged seven.
I've seen it. It's laminated.

Seventy-nine years later,
Nell used it.
'Shh.'
It worked.

Now everyone shushes.
At maximum.

episode.end: There's going to be a vote.
episode.caption:
Someone between the megaphones isn't shouting.

The sun is on its brightest setting, and so are the birds. The rivers run at full volume. Bedtime is set to maximum too, and nobody has reached it yet.

Nell got the planet's only whispering licence at seven, because she was the only child on Max who had never been told to keep it down. She grew up to be the librarian and kept it in a drawer at the issue desk, unspent, for seventy-nine years. The quiet didn't last. The shushing has.

I applied for a licence while I was there. Turned down: nobody heard me apply.

What would you spend one whisper on?

name: Bella
subtitle: every Bella's planet
cover: Everything here is beautiful. By law.
beats: On Bella, everything has to be described as beautiful. It's the law.
The new tax office was declared 'genuinely beautiful' by a man who had clearly been told to.
odd_line: Today's forecast: beautiful rain, followed by beautiful more rain.
story: On Bella, everything has to be described as beautiful, by law. The weather report says beautiful rain. The dentist is beautiful. When the new tax office opened, it was declared 'genuinely beautiful' by a man in a hat who had clearly been told to. The people of Bella are very relaxed about all of this, which is, they would want me to say, beautiful.
rule: Describing anything as 'fine' is a fineable offence.
question: Know a Bella? Send her this. It's beautiful.
extra: The tax office has a five-star rating. Leaving fewer stars is not beautiful.
opener: Everything here is beautiful. By law.

episode.opener:
Everything here
is beautiful.
By law.

beats.text:
The new tax office was declared
'genuinely beautiful'.

By a man who had
clearly been told to.
Teo thinks Nina is beautiful.
So, by law, is the tax office.

'Stunning'? Taken. The dentist.
'Gorgeous'? The bins.

So he rented
the tax office's sign.

spec.sign: YOU ARE MORE|BEAUTIFUL THAN|THE TAX OFFICE

beats.text:
The most romantic sentence
in Bella's history.

spec.sign: YOU ARE MORE|BEAUTIFUL THAN|THE TAX OFFICE

beats.text:
Legally,
an insult to a building.

spec.sign: YOU ARE MORE|BEAUTIFUL THAN|THE TAX OFFICE

episode.end: Every Bella outranks the tax office.
episode.caption:
The tax office would like a word.

Bella is low blue hills, one long view of the sea, and the Beauty Act. It passed in a hurry, the morning after the old mayor called his own wedding 'fine'. Saying 'fine' now costs three compliments, paid in person, and 'not bad' is under review. The tax office has a perfect five-star rating, because leaving fewer stars is not beautiful. Teo was fined for insulting a public building by comparison. Nina had the fine framed. I called the view 'fine' on my first morning. I still owe one compliment.

What would your sign say?

name: Charlie
subtitle: every Charlie's planet
beats: Everyone on Charlie is called Charlie. They tried surnames. Also Charlie.
So they go by what they're holding. Charlie Nothing is having a day off.
odd_line: They tried surnames. Those turned out to be Charlie as well.
story: There are thirty-eight people on Charlie, and all of them are called Charlie. They tried surnames, but those turned out to be Charlie as well. So now everyone goes by whatever they're holding. Charlie Spade does the gardens. Charlie Cup runs the café. Charlie Kettle is not to be trusted with the café. Charlie Nothing is having a day off.
rule: Anyone holding nothing is on holiday and must not be disturbed.
question: How many Charlies do you know?
extra: There was a Charlie Umbrella. It rained once and the whole system nearly collapsed.

beats.text:
They tried surnames.
Also Charlie.

So you go by what you're holding.
Charlie Cup runs the café.

Charlie Nothing
is having a day off.
They called me Charlie Map.

When the café turned thirty,
it gave everyone a free cup.

Thirty-eight Charlie Cups.
On his big day,
nobody knew which was him.

Then they put them down.
Thirty-seven Charlies, on holiday.
He's Charlie Washing-Up now.

episode.caption:
Frame one: find Charlie Cup.

There are thirty-eight people on Charlie, and every one of them is Charlie. Shout 'Charlie!' in the market and the whole street turns round. Babies are Charlie Nothing until they grab something, which is why nobody here wakes a baby. Hands in pockets count as holding nothing, so you can take a day off anywhere.

The morning after the party, thirty-seven Charlies were on holiday, so I dried. For a week I was Charlie Tea Towel.

Welsh villages with too many Joneses did the same thing: Jones the Milk, Jones the Post.

What's your Charlie always holding?

name: Milo
subtitle: every Milo's planet
beats: The soil on Milo is malted chocolate powder, three metres deep.
When it rains, the whole planet smells like the bottom of a school mug.
story: The soil on Milo is malted chocolate powder, three metres deep. Farming is mostly stirring. When the warm rain comes, the ground goes thick and glossy and the whole planet smells like the bottom of a school mug. Everyone on Milo is cheerful and very slightly over-energetic. A few of them eat the ground dry, by the spoonful, which the others consider showing off.
rule: No dunking biscuits in the river.
question: Know a Milo? Do they also eat it dry?
extra: The kettles never go off. There have been no complaints.

episode.opener:
The soil here
is chocolate malt.

beats.text:
Three metres deep.
Farming is mostly stirring.
Those aren't mountains.
They're lumps.

When it rains,
the whole planet smells like
the bottom of a school mug.

Everyone stirs all night.
Nobody wants another mountain.

At dawn the children
go out with spoons.
Lumps are the best bit.

The farmers are very careful
to miss a few.

episode.end: One spoonful of mountain per Milo.
episode.caption:
Look again at the mountains.

The soil on Milo is malted chocolate powder, three metres deep, and the rain falls warm. Everyone here is cheerful and very slightly over-energetic. Morale is excellent. The tallest lump dates from a very good party in 1911. Dunking biscuits in the river is against the law, and a few grown-ups still eat the field dry, by the spoonful, which the others consider showing off.

I went out with the children at dawn. I found four.

On Earth, malt powder lumps the same way: the outside of a clump turns sticky and seals the dry powder in, which is why the lumps crunch.

Lumps: the best bit, or bad stirring?

name: Daisy
subtitle: every Daisy's planet
cover: The flowers know if he loves you.
beats: The fields on Daisy are full of daisies, and each one knows whether he loves you or not.
First dates are held in car parks, well away from any flowers.
odd_line: On a quiet evening the meadow sounds like very light applause, and some booing.
story: The fields on Daisy are covered in daisies, and every one of them knows whether he loves you or not. People stopped pulling petals years ago and just ask the flowers directly. On a quiet evening the meadow sounds like very light applause, with the occasional boo. First dates are held in car parks, well away from any flowers.
rule: Flowers may not be consulted about third parties.
question: Know a Daisy? Send her this one.
extra: Florists here need a licence and a good lawyer.
opener: The flowers know if he loves you.

episode.opener:
The flowers know
if he loves you.

beats.text:
Nobody pulls petals.
You ask, and the meadow claps.
Or boos.

So first dates are held
in the car park.

Bert walked round the meadow
every evening.
The long way.
So did May.

One evening,
Bert took the short way.
So did May.

The meadow still claps
for them.
Most days.

episode.end: Every Daisy gets a round of applause.
episode.caption:
Second time through, look at where Bert and May are standing.

Daisy is mostly meadow, and the daisies are never wrong. They answer out loud: light applause, or some booing. They may not be asked about third parties, which is why florists here need a licence and a good lawyer. The car park was built after one very loud first date. Like ours, they shut at dusk (the name comes from 'day's eye'), and it takes a lot to open them again. There's one path across the middle of the meadow now. It's theirs.

I tried asking about someone back home. Third parties, apparently.

Would you ask the flowers?
